question: What does the acronym ADME stand for in pharmacology?
explanation: ADME represents the four core stages of pharmacokinetics describing how the body handles medications over time. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why is it important for nurses to understand how the body processes drugs?

options.A: To know the chemical makeup of tablets
options.B: To figure out how much each drug costs to make
options.C: To predict when a drug starts working and how long it lasts
options.D: To skip checking patient vital signs

explanation: Knowing how the body processes drugs helps nurses anticipate therapeutic windows and avoid toxicity. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h1)

question: How do most drugs usually cross cell membranes in the body?
explanation: Most drug molecules move naturally down a concentration gradient across cell membranes without needing extra energy. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h2)

question: What happens to an oral drug during the first-pass effect in the liver?

options.A: It is immediately pushed out unchanged through the bile ducts
options.B: Part of the active drug is broken down before reaching the rest of the body
options.C: Cellular receptors multiply to make the drug stronger
options.D: Blood pressure rises rapidly to push the drug into tissues

explanation: Liver enzymes break down a portion of oral medications before they ever reach general circulation. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h2)

question: Which plasma protein is primarily responsible for binding circulating drug molecules?
explanation: Albumin is the major plasma protein that reversibly binds many systemic drug molecules in the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h3)

question: A patient with severe liver disease has low blood albumin. What is likely to happen when they take a protein-bound drug?

options.A: Drug absorption in the gut will stop completely
options.B: The drug will be destroyed before touching any tissues
options.C: The kidneys will instantly wash away all the bound drug
options.D: More free active drug floats in the blood, raising the risk of toxicity

explanation: Fewer binding sites mean a higher proportion of active free drug remains in the blood, magnifying its effects. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h3)

question: Which organ is mainly responsible for breaking down and altering most drugs in the body?
explanation: The liver contains high concentrations of metabolizing enzymes that alter drug structures for easy removal. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is the main goal of Phase II drug metabolism?

options.A: To glue the medication permanently to red blood cells
options.B: To attach a chemical group that makes the drug dissolve in water for easy removal
options.C: To speed up how fast drugs pass through the stomach wall
options.D: To turn inactive drugs into harsh toxins

explanation: Conjugation adds large polar molecules to drug metabolites so they dissolve easily in urine. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h4)

question: Which body system is mainly responsible for getting rid of water-soluble drug waste?
explanation: Renal filtration and urine production clear out the vast majority of water-soluble drug waste from the body. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h5)

question: A patient with weak kidneys is given a normal dose of a drug that leaves the body through urine. What is the most likely result?

options.A: The drug will be instantly destroyed in the stomach
options.B: The drug will quickly leave through the breath
options.C: The drug will have zero effect at all
options.D: The drug builds up in the body and could cause toxicity

explanation: Reduced excretion slows down drug clearance, causing the medication to build up to dangerous levels in the body. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h5)

question: How is the half-life of a medication defined?

options.A: The exact time interval between two missed doses
options.B: The time it takes for the amount of drug in the blood to drop by half
options.C: The time the liver takes to completely destroy a single dose
options.D: The time it takes for a drug to raise blood pressure

explanation: Half-life describes the time it takes for active drug levels in the bloodstream to drop by fifty percent. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h6)

question: Why do drugs with very short half-lives often need to be given frequently or as a continuous drip?

options.A: To keep drug levels in the blood high enough to work
options.B: To wake up enzymes in the liver
options.C: To make the drug stick permanently to cells
options.D: To skip the first-pass effect in the liver

explanation: Frequent administration sustains effective concentration levels before the body eliminates the previous dose. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h6)

question: What is the bioavailability percentage of an intravenous (IV) drug dose?
explanation: Intravenous administration puts the drug directly into the bloodstream, bypassing all barriers like the stomach or gut. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h7)

question: When has a drug reached a steady-state concentration in the body?

options.A: When the amount of drug going in equals the amount leaving
options.B: When the liver stops making enzymes
options.C: When the patient feels completely healed
options.D: When all plasma proteins are fully packed with the drug

explanation: Steady-state occurs when incoming doses balance outgoing elimination, maintaining stable blood concentrations. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h7)

question: Why do elderly patients often need lower drug doses than younger adults?

options.A: Their kidneys and liver clear drugs more slowly
options.B: They have way more albumin protein in their blood
options.C: Their cells completely block all medications
options.D: Their guts absorb medications much faster than normal

explanation: Aging organs process and eliminate drugs more slowly, increasing the risk of cumulative toxicity. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h8)

question: A nurse is caring for a patient taking a drug with a narrow therapeutic range. What is the safest action?

options.A: Give the drug only with heavy meals
options.B: Double the next dose to help the patient recover faster
options.C: Check lab blood levels closely to prevent toxicity
options.D: Stop checking vital signs once the drug is swallowed

explanation: Drugs with narrow therapeutic windows require careful monitoring because effective doses and toxic doses lie close together. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T4#GNS125_U1_T4_h8)
